s-01-words.alt: A list of the words this guide uses, each with its meaning and the rule or chapter that sets it: Locked lines: Our four brand lines whose wording never changes: the tagline, the mission, the reader promise and the editorial commitment. Pillars: Explain, Track, Connect and Act, the four jobs our work does, always in that order. Each pillar has an icon, set with its word beside it. The seven colors: Newsprint, a warm off-white, is our page, and Charcoal carries the words. Pillar Red marks one thing in each view. Prussian, our dark blue, Stone, a mid gray, Verdigris, a muted green, and White support the rest. View: One screen, card, slide or printed page. Working red: The one red a view may spend, on an error the reader must fix, the step they can take now or the point the headline names, in that order. Signature red: The red inside our marks and icons, such as the wordmark’s ampersand and the lockmark’s lever. It never counts as a view’s working red. Token: A named color, size or type setting in our code, such as --oa-color-text-primary-on-newsprint. Builders use the name, and writers can skip the Tokens lines. Kicker: The short line above a headline that says what kind of piece it is. Deck: The line under a headline that says what the piece covers. Hinge headline: A headline that joins a rule to what it produces with our ampersand, as in “The zoning code & the rent.” Hinge divider: A hairline broken by our ampersand, set where a piece turns from how a decision is made to what you can do. Lockup: Our name and marks set together in one fixed arrangement. Our systems atlas: Who Do They Answer To?, our map of who makes public decisions and what shapes them. A loop in it is a chain of causes that returns to where it started, and its ten domains sort every issue by subject, such as elections and representation. Evidence grade: How sure a claim is: documented, well supported, plausible, contested or hypothesis. Illustrative: Our label for anything invented for an example, such as a person, a quote, a place or a figure.
s-01-words.notes: CP-M2, RP-S7: the guide's vocabulary before chapter 01 uses it. Token is defined here for the first time. The atlas glossary's own wording for a feedback loop: a chain of causes that returns to its starting variable.
s-01-words.label: Words this guide uses

s-01-hinge-lines.alt: The ampersand in our name is the hinge, the joint a door swings on. It joins a promise to the action that keeps it, so every piece explains and tracks a decision, then turns to the people who make it and the step a reader can take. Chapter 04 draws the hinge and sets its rules. Then a table of the locked lines, each shown whole with its commitment in bold and its action underlined. Mission: understand, then improve. Reader promise: we explain the decision, then you get a way to take part. Editorial commitment: clarity, our duty, then action, our promise. Pillars: Explain and Track, then Connect and Act. The tagline names the result.
s-01-hinge-lines.notes: From the brand strategy, section 1, approved at Gate 1 (S1). The hinge drawing is chapter 04's. The lead paragraph was the opening's second paragraph until the apply pass; it moved here so the opening keeps the content contract's two paragraphs once A13's paragraph on what nonpartisan means joined it (DR-125).
s-01-hinge-lines.label: The hinge in the locked lines

s-01-pillars.alt: The pillar row: the four pillar icons at 48 px, each with its word beside it, joined by arrows in order: Explain, an open book; Track, a route to a magnifier; Connect, two overlapping rings; Act, a finger pressing a round control. Then each pillar's job and products. 01 Explain: make the rules and their effects understandable. Explainers in the Reform 101 and The Oath series, the atlas's 16 question-first pathways, reports, the weekly briefing newsletter, glossaries and primers. 02 Track: follow the decision and keep its record within reach. Trackers, two series, Dispatch and The Public Record, the atlas Register. 03 Connect: help people reach the office that decides and the evidence it decides on. Guides and call scripts, the Field Notes series, the atlas's view of who can act. 04 Act: give the reader a useful next step. Act pieces in two kinds, case studies in the Proof It Works series, and the closing step on every piece. Last, the compact row at 24 px on a page that serves Track: every icon in one color, and the word Track set bold and underlined.
s-01-pillars.notes: DR-111: the four pillar icons are Civic Line CL-019 Explain, CL-020 Track, CL-021 Connect and CL-022 Act, inlined from the black masters with their geometry untouched and their ink taken through currentColor; each word sits beside its icon, and the current pillar's word is underlined at every size, bold under 48 px. The 48 px row stacks in one column under 48em, with downward arrows, after the creative director's Board 6 review found the phone row dropping its arrow. Products named as the brand's set, with no launch dates or status (DR-91). Product placement follows the brand architecture table (strategy section 3, S2); each series' pillar follows Rule 02.26's series list, and series routes retire (DR-110). s-01-pieces.alt: Four pieces at a phone's text width, one per pillar, each opening with its kicker, turning at the hinge divider to What you can do and ending on one red ask button. Explain: Explainer, utility rates. Why is my electric bill going up? A regulator or a board approves your rate; who decides; then find your rate case. Track: Tracker, Congress. Stop Insider Trading Act Tracker. H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, as the House passed it, would bar members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children from buying individual stocks, and would require photo ID to vote in federal elections. As of November 5, 2026. Six numbered steps, Filed, Hearing, Committee vote, First chamber, Second chamber and President: step 1, Filed, done; step 2, Hearing, never happened; step 3, Committee vote, done; step 4, First chamber, done; step 5, Second chamber, the bill is here now; step 6, President, not yet. Step 5 of 6: Second chamber. A Senate vote to end debate on taking it up got 53 votes on September 30, 2026, short of the 60 it needed, and the bill has stayed on the Senate’s calendar since. Step 2 never happened, because the committee held no hearing on this bill. Its report cites only a hearing held November 19, 2025, before the bill was filed. The committee voted 7 to 4 on January 14, 2026, on a version without the photo ID section, and the House passed both provisions 232 to 198 on July 22, 2026. Then follow this bill. Connect, labeled Illustrative: Guide, Field Notes. Who answers for the repair on your street in Alder County, what to say in 90 seconds, then find your supervisor. Act, labeled Illustrative: Act, how to take part. Alder County votes on backyard cottages March 9; send a comment by March 3.
s-01-pieces.notes: Explain and Track use real atlas copy and records; Connect and Act are invented, each with one Illustrative label at its head (DR-97). Each card is 340 px wide, the text column of a phone; the plate flows so the cards stack on a phone, and the caption carries the width (C-S6). H.R. 7008 named and described whole at its first mention (DR-98). The Track card is a tracker story card, so it takes numbered steps (DR-109) on the six steps with step 6 named President for a federal bill (DR-128); its step states come from the research lead's mapping in round two, and until then it prints the two documented votes. Its kicker stays in words: the Civic Line's Congress icon, CL-025, draws a capitol dome with columns, which Rule 01.6 keeps out of icons.

s-01-uneven.alt: A finding graded documented, reported as the record shows it. After the 2020 election, Donald J. Trump’s presidential campaign asked a federal appeals court to block Pennsylvania’s certified vote totals from taking effect. The court refused on November 27, 2020, noting that the campaign “never alleges that any ballot was fraudulent or cast by an illegal voter.” Lost, Not Stolen, a July 2022 review by eight conservatives, among them two former U.S. senators and three former federal appeals judges, counted 64 cases that Donald Trump and his supporters brought in six battleground states. It found that they “failed to produce substantive evidence to make their case,” and it records one case they won, in Pennsylvania, on far too few votes to change the result. Sources: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, Donald J. Trump for President, Inc. v. Secretary Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, No. 20-3371, opinion filed November 27, 2020, pages 9 and 21, via govinfo.gov; John Danforth and seven co-authors, Lost, Not Stolen: The Conservative Case that Trump Lost and Biden Won the 2020 Presidential Election, July 2022, printed pages 1 and 3, lostnotstolen.org; the 2020 presidential election in Arizona, Georgia, Michigan, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin. Retrieved November 7, 2026. The court issued the opinion as not precedential. The count of 64 cases is the review’s own, and its authors say each of them “has worked in Republican politics, been appointed to office by Republicans, or is otherwise associated with the Party.”

s-02-about.alt: These 21 rules teach writing that sounds like a person talking, and each one shows a sentence before and after the fix. Twelve house rules for every page come with them. Our founder and editor, Dustin Cathcart, set these rules for everything Oath & Action publishes. Sixteen of the 21 rules quote our own work and rewrite the line to pass every rule on the page. Where we found none, we wrote one, and anything we invented carries the Illustrative label. Headings, labels, captions and chart keys may be phrases; every other line on the page is a full sentence. A key: a dotted underline marks what a rule removes, a solid underline marks the repair, and the Illustrative label marks a line invented for the example. The lines we quote come from our brand guide’s fifth edition, our systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, an interactive version of that atlas and early drafts of this guide.

s-02-checklist.alt: Ten questions to ask before you publish, each worded so that yes means pass: 1. Could you say each sentence aloud to a neighbor, with the person who acts named first? 2. Do your sentences change in length and shape as the paragraph goes on? 3. Does the first sentence give the reader a fact or a step, and does the last one end on a fact? 4. Does each sentence say what something is, with no matched pair or “not this, but that” turn? 5. Have you turned every noun that hides a verb back into its verb, and pulled apart every stack of nouns? 6. Does each claim sit at the strength its evidence grade allows, with no word added for force or caution? 7. Are the locked lines exact, and does every invented line, person, place or figure carry the Illustrative label? 8. Does every public policy statistic carry its full source line? 9. Are parties named in words, in the same ink as the text, and is each contested policy called by its neutral name? 10. Are months written as words, numbers under ten spelled out, minus signs true and em dashes gone?
s-02-checklist.label: Before you publish

s-02-25-correct.alt: A table of four rows, what a draft says and what we publish. A sweeping claim, Our democracy is broken, becomes how the system works: Few voters leave their own party’s candidate over an undemocratic stand, so officials who take one face little threat of losing office. Source: Oath & Action’s systems atlas, Who Do They Answer To?, connection L50, partisan loyalty and the risk of losing office, snapshot of October 15, 2026, United States. Retrieved November 6, 2026. From survey experiments with 1,691 respondents (Graham and Svolik, 2020); about 3.5 percent left their own party’s candidate in realistic matchups. A feeling, People are frustrated with Congress, becomes the office that decides: the committee chair decides which bills get a hearing. A slogan, Make your voice heard, becomes an illustrative next step: the hearing is Tuesday at 10 a.m. in Room 4. A side, One party blocked the bill, becomes the structure: H.R. 7008, the Stop Insider Trading Act, as the House passed it, would bar members of Congress, their spouses and dependent children from buying individual stocks, and would require photo ID to vote in federal elections, and it needed 60 votes to move forward in the Senate and got 53, all from Republicans; 45 Democrats and two independents voted no.
s-02-25-correct.notes: Fifth-edition table, kept at Gate 0. Row one (DR-99) is the research lead's first choice, atlas connection L50, graded well supported, kept to the connection so the loop's safe-seat qualification stays out; it touches no ranked-choice voting, primaries or Massachusetts Question 3. Row four names H.R. 7008 whole at its first mention in the chapter (DR-98, BE-M1), documented in the bill texts, with the Congressional Record as the vote's source. DR-126: the count by party sits in the same sentence as both provisions, in Dustin's words from "it needed" to "voted no"; the source line names the Record and marks the party roster (congress-legislators) as secondary, as the research lead's November 6 report read them.

s-02-26-correct.alt: A vocabulary sheet in four parts. Words we use: rule, decision, record, hearing, vote, office, deadline and step. Words we leave out, with what to write instead: genuinely, really, truly, actually, simply and just; leverage as a verb; underscore and reflect; unprecedented; broken, crisis and rigged; stakeholder; empower; fight, battle and front. Series names: Reform 101 and The Oath for Explain, Dispatch and The Public Record for Track, Field Notes for Connect, Proof It Works for Act. Terms we define at first use: hinge; lockmark, our mark of nine nodes, set in four fixed places; lever, which is a place where one change has wide effects; and evidence grade.
